content.title: Solving for Intersections of Linear and Quadratic Functions
content.overview: This lesson teaches how to find the x-coordinates where a line and a parabola intersect. By setting the linear and quadratic expressions equal to each other, you can transform the problem into a standard quadratic equation and solve for the shared x-values.
learning_objectives: Identify the algebraic condition for the intersection of two functions.
Convert a system of linear and quadratic equations into a single quadratic equation in standard form.
Use the discriminant to determine the number of intersection points.
Apply the quadratic formula to calculate the exact x-coordinates of intersection.

sections.title: The Principle of Intersection
sections.content: An intersection point occurs where two functions share the same x-value and the same y-value. To find these points algebraically, set the linear expression equal to the quadratic expression: f(x) = g(x). This creates a single-variable equation that represents the horizontal positions (x-values) where the graphs meet.

sections.title: The Set-Subtract-Solve Strategy
sections.content:
To solve for intersection, follow three main steps: 1. Set the expressions equal (e.g., mx + b = ax^2 + bx + c). 2. Move all terms to one side of the equation to set it equal to zero, resulting in the standard form Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0. 3. Solve this new quadratic equation using factoring or the quadratic formula.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Set Equal, Move Terms to One Side, Calculate Discriminant, Apply Quadratic Formula.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/2430c82d-17df-4043-a0c8-ee8a80539932-1786505847300-107.webp)

sections.title: Predicting Intersections with the Discriminant
sections.content: Before solving fully, the discriminant (D = b^2 - 4ac) of the combined equation tells you how many times the functions intersect. If D > 0, there are two distinct real intersection points. If D = 0, the line is tangent to the parabola, touching at exactly one point. If D < 0, the line and parabola never intersect in the real coordinate plane.

worked_examples.question: Find the x-values where f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1 and g(x) = 2x - 3 intersect.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Set the functions equal: x^2 - 4x + 1 = 2x - 3. Step 2: Move all terms to the left side: x^2 - 4x - 2x + 1 + 3 = 0, which simplifies to x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0. Step 3: Identify coefficients: a=1, b=-6, c=4. Step 4: Use the quadratic formula: x = [-(-6) ± √((-6)^2 - 4(1)(4))] / (2*1). Step 5: Simplify: x = [6 ± √(36 - 16)] / 2 = [6 ± √20] / 2. Since √20 = 2√5, x = (6 ± 2√5) / 2 = 3 ± √5. The intersection x-values are 3 + √5 and 3 - √5.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to move all terms to one side before applying the quadratic formula.
Only providing one x-value when the discriminant is positive and two intersections exist.
Sign errors when subtracting the linear expression from the quadratic expression.
Confusing the intersection x-values with the y-intercepts of the individual functions.
exam_tips: If the answer choices are radicals, use the quadratic formula immediately after setting the equation to zero.
Check your work using the sum of roots (-b/a) or product of roots (c/a) on your combined quadratic equation.
If a question asks for the 'number' of intersections rather than the values, only calculate the discriminant.
content.recap: To find where a line and parabola meet, set their equations equal, move all terms to one side to form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, and solve for x. The discriminant determines if they meet twice, once, or never.

knowledge_claims.content: An intersection point of two functions f(x) and g(x) is a coordinate pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations simultaneously.
The first step in finding intersection x-values is to set the linear expression equal to the quadratic expression.
After setting expressions equal, all terms must be moved to one side to create a quadratic equation in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
The discriminant used to check for intersection points is calculated as b^2 - 4ac from the combined quadratic equation.
If the discriminant of the combined equation is greater than zero, the line and parabola intersect at exactly two distinct points.
If the discriminant of the combined equation is exactly zero, the line is tangent to the parabola and they share exactly one intersection point.
If the discriminant of the combined equation is less than zero, there are no real x-values where the line and parabola intersect.
The x-coordinates of intersection can be found using the quadratic formula: x = (-b ± √(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a.
A common error is failing to change the signs of the linear terms when moving them to the side of the quadratic terms.
The validity of intersection x-values can be verified by ensuring the sum of the calculated roots equals -b/a from the combined equation.
The validity of intersection x-values can be verified by ensuring the product of the calculated roots equals c/a from the combined equation.
To find the y-coordinate of an intersection, substitute the solved x-value back into either the original linear or quadratic equation.
